newsitem.title: GUATEMALA: GUATEMALANS BURIED IN SCRAMBLE AFTER TRAGEDY.
newsitem.headline: GUATEMALANS BURIED IN SCRAMBLE AFTER TRAGEDY.

text.p: Burial of Guatemala's soccer stadium victims came too quickly on Friday for the shocked families, who last saw their loved ones with excited faces before a big soccer match.

Many of the dead were packed into cheap vaults in Guatemala City's cemetery and bricked up by funeral workers darting around with wheelbarrows of cement. One inconsolable woman who was burying her husband and teenage son had to be gently pried from each casket before they were slid horizontally into the flower-draped wall.
Bearing wreaths, the grieving jostled for a place at the two above-ground burial vaults where more than 10 simultaneous funerals took place early on Friday.

Most of the up to 82 victims of the tragedy were poor, suffocated under a cascade of bodies in the cheap terraces of the Mateo Flores stadium just before Wednesday night's scheduled Guatemala-Costa Rica World Cup qualifying game.
They were buried too in the cheap section -- the "niche area" on the fringes of the cemetery where bodies are slotted in at $15 each for six years before they are removed to a common pit.
One group of casket bearers in tattered clothes bore their dead, followed by a thin, elderly woman carrying a bag of cement on her head.
The raised voices of Catholic priests and evangelical ministers competed for listeners on the sunny morning. Cemetery officials frantically checked lists to ensure each coffin found its proper niche.
The dead arrived in hearses in tin or wood coffins at the heads of snaking funeral corteges of cars and rusty pick-up trucks. The cemetery was booked up for burials all day.

Seeking to capture the public grief, television cameras zig-zagged through the crowd like shark fins through the surf. Many of the 1,000 mourners, weeping and looking drawn after a nightlong wake, tried to make sense of the fatal night.

"There are all these gangs and gangsters ... this happened because of the forgery of tickets," said Ana Hernandez, whose cousin Hugo Mendozaba, 41, was buried on Friday, leaving behind a widow and six children.

On radio talk shows, in streets and taxis, in lines at the cemetery, authorities were blamed for slapdash security at the Mateo Flores stadium and the entry of hundreds of people with forged tickets who surged in unchecked.
Angry and confused, mourners and the public in general demanded better explanations from the government as to why the soccer game turned into a calamity.

President Alvaro Arzu, in a solemn broadcast to the nation late on Thursday, pledged to find the cause of the deaths and named a high-level commission including the interior and health ministers to report back within 15 days.
